newsitem.title: DUBAI: At least 30 said dead in haj blaze in Saudi Arabia.
newsitem.headline: At least 30 said dead in haj blaze in Saudi Arabia.

text.p: At least 30 haj pilgrims, all believed to be Pakistanis, died on Tuesday in a blaze at a tent compound near the Islamic holy city of Mecca, Pakistan's ambassador to Saudi Arabia said.

"Thirty are believed to be dead. We fear they may all be Pakistanis," Ambassador Shahed Amin, who visited the site of the fire in Mena, told Reuters from Mecca by telephone. "There are probably more (dead) but I cannot speak for other nationalities."
The official Saudi Press Agency said the fire started at 11.45 a.m. (0845 GMT) at a bridge linking Mecca and Mena, and that heavy winds spread the blaze to Mena -- site of the tent compound.
George Joseph, deputy chief of mission at the Indian Embassy in Riyadh, said the fire was put out by 2.30 p.m. (1130 GMT).
The cause of the fire was not immediately known.
The fatal blaze is the latest tragedy to strike Moslems on pilgrimage to Mecca, their holiest shrine. Able-bodied Moslems are obliged to make the haj at least once if they can afford it.
The worst of recent Mecca tragedies was a stampede during the 1990 haj in which 1,426 pilgrims were crushed to death in a tunnel.
In 1994, 270 pilgrims were killed during a stampede at Mena, where pilgrims hurl stones at three piles of rocks symbolising the devil.
Joseph said pilgrims affected by Tuesday's fire were being evacuated from the plain at Mena and moving back the 11 km (seven miles) towards Mecca.
"People are being evacuated from Mena back to Mecca, which is the only safe place," he told Reuters by telephone from the Saudi capital Riyadh.
"Some Indian tent camps were burnt. We have no idea if any of our people were hurt," Joseph said, adding the embassy had been flooded with calls from concerned relatives of pilgrims.
Amin, the Pakistani ambassador, said about 30,000 people were in the Pakistani camp. "There has been extensive damage to about 50,000 tents" across the tent city, he said.
Amin said: "The fire is under control and the situation is calm and orderly now."
Earlier, Arab and Iranian witnesses had said by telephone from Mecca that thick clouds of black smoke billowing over Mena could be seen from the city.
One witness told CNN the smoke turned day into night and there was "mass hysteria" among the pilgrims.
Witnesses told Reuters they heard the wailing sound of ambulance sirens and fire engines rushing to the scene. Helicopters from the fire department flew overhead, they added.

They said the fire had slowed down the movement of pilgrims from about 100 countries who began leaving Mecca on Tuesday after dawn prayers at the Grand Mosque where they circled Kaaba seven times, the first haj ritual.
Saudi Arabia, custodian of Islam's two holiest shrines, has spent $18.6 billion in the last decade on expanding sites in Mecca and surrounding areas.
Saudi officials had said they were doing their best to ensure a safe haj. They have urged the pilgrims to abide by security instructions, especially in usually congested areas.
Cameras installed on main roads, bridges and tunnels monitor pilgrims' movements to ensure that haj proceeds peacefully.
